comments.name: Matías
comments.body: As a medical journalist for Medscape in Spanish, I covered a session on antidepressant deprescribing at the 2023 Argentine Congress of Psychiatry. I believe the following paragraph of the story offers a potential framework for medication withdrawal—always under professional supervision: "Although most clinical practice guidelines lack precise strategies for gradually tapering antidepressant medications or clear criteria to distinguish withdrawal symptoms from depressive relapses, one viable approach is recommended by The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry: tapering by 25% if the risk is low (treatments under six months, long half-life drugs, and no history of withdrawal) and by 5% to 10% if the risk is high. The Royal College of Psychiatrists in the UK proposes dose-reduction schedules that can stretch over several months, stepping down to doses below 1 mg before stopping the antidepressant entirely. Other strategies involve switching to fluoxetine, antiepileptics, or haloperidol as a 'bridging step' prior to complete discontinuation, though these rely more on expert opinion than on clear consensus."

comments.name: Pdxjc
comments.body:
I've been on an SSRI for 50 of my 69 years. In my 20s I had severe depression due to a very traumatic childhood, followed by sexual abuse, and 30 years of alcoholism. Sober 19 years now. No doctor has ever suggested I try adult life without them, and two actually discouraged me from trying to taper off.

I realized just in the last few years that I don't have many feelings anymore. My sister died 2 years ago, and my grief was almost completely blunted. I've had to put down 2 beloved cats, and another died in my arms. No tears. I have almost no romantic or sexual feelings. I feel like I'm faking almost all reactions. I thought it might be due to giving up my tried and true source of euphoria--alcohol--but now I wonder if it's a near-lifetime of antidepressants.

I tried to taper off my SSR I5 years ago, and who I became was a frightening mix of rage and hopelessness. I've been reading about micro-tapering, and think I'll try it once I have a particularly stressful situation out of the way. I appreciate this article!

comments.name: NSColumbus
comments.body:
There are challenges in many directions. On the one hand, each patient's struggle is unique. Anxiety in autism is different from autism with Tourette's or post-traumatic anxiety. People may not recognize the differences between their circumstances and someone else's. All magic has a cost, and any medication has some risk - the question is, is the disease worse than the medication?
On the other hand, too many meds became available too freely. To prescribe the acne drug isotretinoin, you have to register in a federal program and document what you are doing. To prescribe lexapro, you write an order. This is upside down. I don't know Cam's story, but Klonopin on top of an SSRI is a major combination. Using a benzodiazapine daily like that should have been highly monitored and regulated, not left to the patient. Addiction to benzos is real and can be as bad or worse than alcoholism. 
You are right, we physicians need to do better, and we need to listen to our patient community. But that does not mean that MAHA approaches will work for everyone or anyone. We all need to listen first, truly listen. Cam hasn't been listened to for years, and now it sounds like he might be done listening, too.

comments.name: Skye6206
comments.body:
As a retired psychiatrist, I find this column equal parts biased and dispiriting (?depressing).  Anti-psychiatric jeremiads have a long history, with Scientology led efforts at the forefront.

I understand why.  Psychiatry is an imperfect science, the medications have side effects.  When they come out, we do not know the long term effects of taking them (do we know the long term effects of the glp-1 meds we are all on).  And yes, it is easier and cheaper to write for a medication than to do hours of long-term therapy, knowing there are some conditions that really need medication, and no amount of therapy will fix it.  Doctors like easier and cheaper.  So do patients.

But the author has no knowledge of the history here.  SSRIs, imperfect as they are, are no more effective for depression or anxiety than the tricyclics that preceded them.  But an overdose of tricyclics was often fatal.  SSRI overdoses are not.  That was a game changer.  Now you had a med you coud give elderly people that did not drop their blood pressure or put them to sleep.  You had an alternative to ECT (shock therapy).  The downside to treatment was less, which certainly could lead to overprescription.
But the author's POV fits in perfectly with MAHA, even if she does not see it.  The take home message is do not trust science, be cynical about good intents, and the treatment is probably worse than the illness.
I do not know anyone who has died of SSRI withdrawal.  I know plenty who died of depression.

comments.name: Eli
comments.body:
This is a very important thoughtful and engaging article and I am grateful for it. Cam may be an influencer yet his story is not unique. Countless people have been medicated since before they could even understand the effects of the medication and it affected them long-term to the point they relied on an ever expanding cascade of medications, which ultimately caused more problems than the initial symptoms. I know from direct personal experience as well, the difference is that I'm not as skilled at cold plunges. 

The worst issue that we must deal with is avoiding withdrawal through safe tapering. As with Cam's experience and the information from Dr Goldberg, I didn't know how to taper and no one told me how nor even that it was necessary. This plunged me into a horrible withdrawal I never fully healed from, including Post-SSRI Sexual Dysfunction I live with today. I know it was withdrawal because my symptoms were not experienced before I took the meds. Protracted SSRI withdrawal has not been studied in depth as most SSRI trials are short term. 

The paragraph I resonated with the most was the critique of MAHA's hypocrisy; that their proposals of studying SSRI withdrawal and other adverse effects like PSSD would require more institutional medicine funding, yet they are cutting healthcare and research funds. I believe our government should funnel more money into healthcare research to support all patients, especially the ones harmed by the pharmaceutical industry.

comments.name: Christopher

Coming off psych meds, especially anti-depressants and anti-psychotics such as Seroquel and Risperdal, is incredibly hard the longer you take them.  I start transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS; look it up) next month.  I'm hoping it will permanently be my ticket out of darkness.  And while I an grateful to the drugs for dragging me out of the pit, I can't fathom being on them for the rest of my life.  

There are other modalities when it comes to mental healthcare--ketamine or psilocybin therapy with a trained psychiatrist or nurse, as well as TMS .  I wish more mental health providers would discuss them with their patients instead of just prescribing a pill that's only really ever a bandage.  

My heart goes out to Cam.  I can't blame him for taking charge of his life and wanting to manage it on his own.

I teach in a small public university, and I am sure one's mileage may vary & terms and conditions apply by institution, but I frankly have not seen or felt all the push of identity politics or pronouns or woke-ness as strongly as the media might portray. It is present but not all pervasive. Rather than campus battles over politics, we have mostly quiet classrooms and labs. Perhaps my audience is more working adults or career minded students.

Similarly, I am not sure if there is an undercurrent of self sorting by major, club, fraternity or sorority. Perhaps it's more visible in the Ivy League, elite liberal arts, Christian colleges or large state universities. 

So perhaps students self sort in enrollment which may be by design (i.e, the student and family choosing an institution for its leanings or mission) or perhaps by accident in some cases ("who knew these Ivy League types were so liberal!") . . 

But I can also say you very often have to teach a survey course covering everything on a given subject in a semester, especially if you are following your department or institutions student learning outcomes, and there is often little time for polarizing commentary or gearing lectures or content for a particular ideology, even if wished to.

IMHO, that's an invitation to friction and problems. And "you don't want these problems". . . The goal is to get through the semester covering all the material (which in many fields does not even lend itself to political ideology).

I have no children, so can only apply my own experience to this column.

When I went off to college in 1970, my parents wanted me to get a liberal arts education and I wound up at Bard College in the Hudson River Valley.  The Vietnam War was in full swing, so anti-war liberalism was the norm on campus.

Now, reading this piece, I'm struck by necessary information that was left out.  For example, about 58% of all American undergrads are women, while only about 42% are men.  Women at that age are skewing liberal, while men are skewing conservative.  I dare say that an academically capable young conservative man applying to colleges isn't going to apply to Bard, even though he could get a wonderful education there.  If he wants a liberal arts education, he'll apply to Hillsdale.  He could then spend four years believing in Reaganomics and reading Ayn Rand.  Young liberals aren't going to want to do that.

With today's extreme polarization, what is described in this column is to be expected.  With college costing as much as it does, students are entitled to make it as positive an experience as possible.

Any meeting of polarized minds is not likely to occur at college.  It will take universal service after college, with deliberate mixing of liberals and conservatives, city folk and country folk.  It's a good idea that will almost certainly not happen.

comments.name: Guy Carden
comments.body:
Part 1 of 2:

“Until recently, attacking civilian energy infrastructure was unacceptable.”

Mr. Wallace-Wells cites a 2026 West Point study,  but his own essay gives a highly non-standard version of the relevant international law and military history.

“They used to call this kind of thing a war crime.” 

Power plants and the power grid in general are “dual use,” important to civilians, but also important to military, government, communications, munitions production and a range of other legitimate military objectives. International law permits you to attack dual-use infrastructure as long as the civilian cost is proportionate to the military advantage.

Since before World War II, the enemy’s power system has generally been regarded as a legitimate high-priority target, with the military advantage outweighing the cost to civilians. West Point’s Lieber Institute gives a useful overview:
https://lieber.westpoint.edu/attacking-power-infrastructure-under-international-humanitarian-law/

“... for decades it has been rare for great powers to openly target energy supply...”

That is incorrect.   Specifics in Part 2.

comments.name: Guy Carden
comments.body:
Part 2 of 2:

“Until recently, attacking civilian energy infrastructure was unacceptable.”

Mr. Wallace-Wells cites a 2026 West Point study,  but his own essay gives a highly non-standard version of the relevant international law and military history.

“They used to call this kind of thing a war crime.” 

Since before World War II, the enemy’s power system has generally been regarded as a legitimate high-priority target.  Details in Part 1.

“... for decades it has been rare for great powers to openly target energy supply...”

That is incorrect.

In WW II, we didn’t target the German and Japanese electrical systems;  but that was because we thought it was too hard a target, not because we had any doubts about legality.

In Korea (1950-53), we claim to have destroyed 90% of the enemy generating capacity.  In Vietnam (mostly 1965-68 and 1972), 85-90%.  In the first Iraq War (1991), “over 90%”.  In the Kosovo action (1999), the Air Force reports “...stealth fighters struck the electrical plant at Novi Sad, which cut off electricity to 70 percent of Serbia.”

In the second Iraq War (2003), we made a deliberate attempt to minimize damage to the electrical system, because we foresaw correctly that we would need to fix it after the war.  That represents an exception to the historical pattern.

As Mr. Wallace-Wells reports, Russia and Ukraine have been targeting electrical systems since 2022, returning to the established post WW II pattern.

One key piece that stands out to me in this conversation is that we all react to information differently.  Admittedly, I was not familiar with the Dialog matter and Ezra's supposed inclusivity in Thiel's secret society.  I honestly had to look it up.  But as politically engaged as many of us are with Ezra's work and many others, I think we fail to take into account the information we take in consistently.  In Ezra's recent interview with Maggie Haberman, she made a valid point about how people in today's day and age can subscribe to any information stream they want and believe those experts or pundits without question.  We as an educated, politically engaged population are equally subject to those information streams as well, for better or worse.  

I do believe Ezra, that he is not part of a secret society.  His explanation is fine for me.  I agree that Ezra could have done more in challenging Rufo on many of his stances even if that was not the goal.  But more importantly, we all can do a better job at listening to those we disagree with (listen to Ross Douthat's guests) and be better for it.  We must learn to talk with one another instead of confining ourselves in our own information spaces.  Believe and stand for what we believe.  But do it in grace, honesty, and empathy.  This is my key takeaway from this conversation and is a lesson we all can apply to our lives.

Somehow, we’re capable of spending hundreds of billions of dollars every year for “defense,” but can’t seem to find money help bring back those who sacrificed everything. 

I can speak from personal experience, as well, about what an extraordinary human being Justin Taylan is; he and his nonprofit (Pacific Wrecks) have worked tirelessly to help my family try to gain more insights into my grandfather’s mission, disappearance and possible location. 

As admirable and selfless as Justin’s efforts are, he shouldn’t even need to step in; the government completely and utterly fails its duty to honor those who gave their lives for all of us.

Such a freedom w/that.  Certainly in Shakespeare - as the article says - understanding what you're saying. The Brits are brought up with this which IMHO is why they get it right. It's not like TV writing with its meaning between the lines. You really do need that platform of breath & a steady column of it to keep the line going & own the meaning of what you're saying. Not sure if what I'm saying is clear but I will say that after you did the exercises that Liz Dixon (RIP) had you could feel that you had a richer and more expressive vocal instrument which IMHO is usually the weakest trick in the actor's bag of tricks because of miked performances etc. Liz Dixon worked with many actors e.g. Michael Douglas (won an Academy Award) & Lindsay Crouse (also nominated after working with her on Prince of the City) but what Liz loved most was being brought to Checkers for a weekend to work with the 'Iron Lady'. 
So kudos to all vocal coaches - we need 'em.

comments.body: As I retired youth services librarian, we used to call books like "Diary of a Wimpy Kid" hybrids: a hybrid of a traditional novel and a graphic novel. I am not sure if this is the preferred term now. The beauty of hybrids is that they often appeal to kids who are choosier readers; those who need many illustrations to help them enjoy the story, kids who struggle with reading, or kids who need fast paced books. Other funny hybrids I would suggest are "Dog Man" by Dav Pilkey, "Stick Dog" by Tom Watson, "Max and the Midknights" by Lincoln Peirce, and a wonderful mystery series, "Timmy Failure" by Stephan Pastis. I distinguish hybrids from graphic novels, as hybrids tend to have more pages with just text, and graphic novels have panels and usually illustrations on every page. Many kids who love hybrids also love graphic novels, so I would second "Mexikid" too!
